questions.q: Identify the inciting incident in "फेंकू उल्हनिहु" that sets the narrator's investigation into Phenku's past in motion.
questions.a: The inciting incident is the narrator noticing Phenku's unusual method of making puris—flinging them into the air ("फेंकू उल्हनिहु")—which prompts his curiosity about the cook's origins. A wrong answer (e.g., "the narrator hiring Phenku" or "the colonial officer anecdote") reveals the student confuses backstory with the narrative's present-time trigger, indicating they haven't distinguished between chronological order and narrative order.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Yashpal chooses first-person narration from the master's perspective rather than Phenku's or a third-person omniscient voice.
questions.a: First-person master-narration creates dramatic irony: the narrator believes he is studying Phenku, but the narrative structure reveals the master's own colonial mindset and class blindness. The reader sees what the narrator cannot. A wrong answer focusing only on "authenticity" or "personal touch" misses the satirical function—the structure itself performs the critique by trapping us in the master's limited perspective.

questions.q: Map the following five events onto a plot diagram (exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution): (A) Narrator learns Phenku's wife calls him "उल्हनिहु", (B) Narrator watches Phenku make puris, (C) Phenku recounts the colonial officer demanding "फेंकू", (D) Narrator reflects on "रखेह की रखेह", (E) Phenku serves puris silently at the end.
questions.a: Correct mapping: B (exposition) → A (inciting incident/rising action) → C (rising action peak) → D (climax: philosophical realization) → E (falling action/resolution: silent service as resistance). A wrong sequence (e.g., placing C before A) shows the student follows chronological logic rather than narrative logic—the colonial anecdote is a flashback positioned for maximum ironic impact, not temporal order.

questions.q: Compare the narrative pacing of the puri-making scene (detailed, sensory) with the colonial officer anecdote (summarized, reported speech). What does this pacing contrast reveal about Yashpal's thematic priorities?
questions.a: The slow, sensory pacing of the puri scene centers Phenku's skilled labor and dignity in the present; the rushed, reported anecdote marginalizes the colonial master's voice, reducing his authority to a ridiculous memory. This structural choice enacts the story's theme: the "servant's" craft outlasts the "master's" power. A student who only notes "one is long, one is short" without linking pacing to power dynamics misses the analytical leap from form to meaning.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "The story's open ending—Phenku continuing to serve puris silently—is a narrative failure because it resolves no conflict." Defend or refute using structural evidence.
questions.a: Refute. The open ending IS the resolution: it structurally mirrors the exposition (Phenku making puris) but transformed by the reader's new knowledge. The conflict (narrator's curiosity vs. Phenku's opacity) resolves not through revelation but through the narrator's—and reader's—shifted understanding. A student calling it "incomplete" expects conventional closure (conflict solved, mystery answered) and misses how satirical narratives use structural circularity to imply ongoing resistance.

questions.q: Write a 50-word "missing scene" inserted between the colonial officer anecdote and the final reflection that maintains Yashpal's narrative voice and satirical tone. Use first-person narration and dialogue only.
questions.a: Sample: "मैंने पूछा, 'फिर वह अँग्रेज़ गया कहाँ?' फेंकू ने पूरी हवा में उछाली। 'जहाँ से आया था।' 'और तुम?' 'यहीं।' उसने चटनी का कटोरा बढ़ाया। 'लीजिए, ठंडी न हो जाए।'" A poor answer uses third-person, explains feelings, or resolves the mystery—violating the story's rules: master asks, Phenku deflects, labor continues, dignity intact.
